paper_title: DiffResearch: Accelerating Deep Research with Diffusion Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Deep research systems iteratively plan, gather evidence, synthesize, and revise, making end-to-end latency a key bottleneck for interactive use. Almost all production systems are built on autoregressive (AR) language models and inherit left-to-right decoding in planning and long-form writing. We present DiffResearch, an open multi-agent deep research framework that places a diffusion language model (dLLM) at the core of every stage, and measure how a diffusion backbone changes latency and report quality. Holding the agentic scaffold, retrieval code, prompts, and evaluation fixed, we swap the backbone between an open diffusion model and a comparable AR model. Across 100 Deep Research Bench tasks, the diffusion backbone is roughly 6 times faster end-to-end, driven by order-of-magnitude reductions in planning and writing. We further introduce dFast, a decomposition mode that reads intermediate denoising states and extracts subqueries before generation finishes, providing a 1.99 times median speedup for decomposition in isolation with no loss of report quality. On the benchmark's RACE rubric, dFast obtains the best overall score among the three configurations. Finally, in a public system-level leaderboard snapshot, an instance built on a stronger diffusion model ranks above several commercial systems. We release DiffResearch under an Apache-2.0 license.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The past two years have seen deep research (DR) systems emerge as flagship application of large language models (LLMs). Commercial products such as OpenAI Deep Research (OpenAI, 2025), Gemini Deep Research (Citron, 2024), and Perplexity Deep Research (Perplexity, 2025), alongside growing body of open-source frameworks (The LangChain Team, 2025; Zheng et al., 2025), autonomously orchestrate multi-step web exploration, *Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Industry Track. 1 targeted retrieval, and higher-order synthesis to turn large amounts of online information into citationrich reports. Among the tasks these systems perform, scientific literature review is one of the most demanding: review requires balanced thematic coverage, faithful attribution, the identification of competing methodological camps, and coherent narrative that situates each work within the broader landscape. As Deep Research Bench (Du et al., 2026) and similar evaluations (Coelho et al., 2026; Yifei et al., 2026) have shown, the strongest agents now approach the quality of human analysts on PhD-level tasks across dozens of fields. Despite this progress, almost all production DR agents share one architectural backbone: they are built on autoregressive LLMs (Brown et al., 2020; Touvron et al., 2023; OpenAI, 2023) and inherit the same left-to-right, single-pass decoding that governs their token generators. This shapes both how reviews are written and how fast they are produced. writing agent drafts each section sequentially, with limited ability to revise earlier passages once new evidence arrives later, so that errors in early structural decisions can propagate through the rest of the review. The same sequential bottleneck constrains the orchestration layer: when an agent must emit several search queries to fan out retrieval over distinct facets of the literature, autoregressive decoding produces them one token at time, and downstream retrieval is dispatched only after generation completes. For an interactive research assistant, every one of these stages is on the critical path, and their latencies add up. Diffusion language models (Li et al., 2022; Austin et al., 2021; Lou et al., 2024) offer complementary generation paradigm: text is refined through iterative denoising that updates an entire sequence in parallel across small number of steps. Recent systems such as LLaDA (Nie et al., 2025), Dream (Ye et al., 2025), and Mercury (Inception Labs et al., 2025) suggest that diffusion LLMs can approach the quality of autoregressive models while offering advantages in generation speed and global coherence. Yet diffusion LLMs have largely been evaluated in standalone settings such as chat and coding; their integration into agentic pipelines that interleave planning, retrieval, and iterative refinement remains underexplored, and the practical latency consequences of that integration have not been measured directly. We introduce DiffResearch,1 an open deep research framework in which every agent is an instance of diffusion LLM. Our aim is to measure what changes when the backbone is diffusion rather than autoregressive, with the rest of the system held fixed. The framework combines standard agentic scaffold (intent classification, query reformulation, planning, retrieval, writing, and an optional judge) with diffusion-based writing stage that drafts and refines the full review in parallel rather than section by section. It supports two operating modes: full mode that runs the base pipeline once, and an iterative subquery-decomposition (fast) mode in which diffusion decomposition agent produces the full subquery set within single denoising pass, with usable subqueries read from intermediate denoising states before generation completes. Because all subqueries become available at once, their retrieval calls could in principle be dispatched together; in our controlled runs retrieval is rate-limited to one request per second, so we report the decompositionstage speedup in isolation and leave parallel retrieval dispatch to future work. The framework exposes one agent abstraction with interchangeable backbones, so we can keep the whole scaffold fixed and change only the generator, and any difference can be attributed to the decoding paradigm rather than to unrelated system changes. Our contributions are as follows: An open diffusion-native deep research framework with two operating modes and single agent abstraction whose backbone can be set to diffusion or an autoregressive model, enabling controlled comparison. direct latency comparison between diffusion and autoregressive backbones in an otherwise identical pipeline on Deep Re1Previous presentation: ICML 2026 AI4Science (https: //openreview.net/forum?id=EGb0wlKWVz). This version adds controlled AR-backbone comparison, dFast analysis, language-specific diagnostics, and source-grounding audit. Code: https://github.com/alanrbtx/DiffResearch. search Bench, showing roughly 6 end-toend speedup concentrated in the planning and writing stages. fast decomposition mode that extracts the subquery set from intermediate denoising states, cutting decomposition latency by about half (1.99 at the median over 100 queries) while keeping downstream report quality; in our runs it also gives the best RACE overall score, but no additional end-to-end latency reduction over standard diffusion generation. system-level leaderboard snapshot in which an instance of the same framework built on stronger diffusion model ranks above several publicly listed commercial deep research systems, without isolating the effect of diffusion decoding.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Deep research agents. Commercial systems (OpenAI, 2025; Citron, 2024; Perplexity, 2025) and open-source frameworks (The LangChain Team, 2025; Zheng et al., 2025) integrate multistep reasoning, retrieval, and synthesis to produce long-form, citation-grounded outputs. Benchmarks such as Deep Research Bench (Du et al., 2026), DeepResearchGym (Coelho et al., 2026), and ResearchQA (Yifei et al., 2026) evaluate these systems on complex, multi-domain tasks. Most rely on autoregressive LLMs (Brown et al., 2020; Touvron et al., 2023; OpenAI, 2023) and inherit the constraints of sequential decoding. Prior work has explored agentic scaffolds that decompose tasks into modular planning, retrieval, and evaluation components (Wang et al., 2024; Xi et al., 2025), judge models that assess output quality (Zheng et al., 2023), and retrieval-augmented generation to ground outputs in external sources (Lewis et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2023b). Diffusion language models. Diffusion-based text models (Li et al., 2022; Austin et al., 2021; Lou et al., 2024) generate through iterative denoising, refining an entire sequence in parallel across few steps, and naturally support structure-first generation and iterative error correction (Li et al., 2022; Gong et al., 2023). Recent open models such as LLaDA (Nie et al., 2025) and Dream (Ye et al., 2025), and the Mercury family (Inception Labs et al., 2025), show that diffusion LLMs can approach autoregressive quality while offering speed 2 and global-coherence advantages. To our knowledge, no prior work has measured how diffusion decoding affects the end-to-end latency and report quality of an agentic deep research pipeline under controlled backbone swap. Efficient generation. large literature improves generation efficiency through speculative decoding, caching, distillation, and parallel decoding. Our fast decomposition mode is complementary and is not speculative decoding: it does not use draft model, but instead reads the diffusion models own intermediate denoising states and stops once valid structured output is available.

sections.title: 3 System Design
sections.content: 3.1 Multi-Agent Diffusion Pipeline DiffResearch is multi-agent framework in which every agent is an instance of diffusion LLM. The system is organized as small, explicit pipeline rather than monolithic chain; we deliberately avoid heavy orchestration abstractions (Chase, 2022) that obscure data flow and make latency budgets and retry behavior hard to reason about. Each agent is Python class that inherits from common backbone and implements single generate method. The backbone is interchangeable: Hugging Face diffusion runtime serving google/diffusiongemma-26B-A4B-it for diffusion-native deployment, or Hugserving ging Face google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it for the baseline. The controlled comparison in Section 5 relies on this: changing the backbone leaves every prompt, retrieval call, and evaluation step unchanged. autoregressive runtime Nine agents cover query formatting, planning, plan-checking, relevance filtering, information extraction, summarization, complexity assessment, query decomposition, and judging. Outputs are kept minimal and machine-parseable: binary flags for routing decisions, newline-separated query lists from the decomposition and judge agents, and freeform text only where downstream consumption requires it. Per-agent decoding budgets are exposed through the constructor; for example, the relevance and complexity agents use short budget appropriate to their binary outputs, while the summarization agent uses substantially larger budget to accommodate full review drafts. The base pipeline has five core stages (intent classification, query reformulation, planning, retrieval, and writing), with judging as an optional 3 sixth stage. The intent agent routes query to web channel or an academic channel and emits label with logged-but-not-propagated rationale. The reformulation agent rewrites the query into retrieval-friendly search strings (Wang et al., 2023; Jagerman et al., 2023) while preserving the original information need verbatim. The planning agent (Wei et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2023) produces structured outline: main sections, two-to-four subpoints each, and an explicit list of key concepts to cover. The outline serves both as the writing target and as the reference for plan-checking. The writing agent drafts the review conditioned on the plan and the retrieved corpus through diffusion-style refinement. The judge (Zheng et al., 2023) compares the review against the plan and corpus along plan adherence, citation faithfulness (Gao et al., 2023a; Liu et al., 2023), and coverage completeness.

sections.title: 3.2 Retrieval Backends
sections.content: Retrieval grounds every claim and is treated as first-class component. The web channel issues queries through the Serper API (Serper, n.d.) and extracts page content into plain text. The academic channel issues parallel calls to the Semantic Scholar API (Kinney et al., 2023), for broad peerreviewed coverage and citation-graph signals, and the arXiv API (arXiv, n.d.), for timely preprints; results are deduplicated by DOI and arXiv identifier and merged into single ranked list. In all cases retrieval is performed by deterministic API calls with no LLM in the loop, which keeps it fast, cacheable, and easy to ablate. For the controlled benchmark runs in this paper, retrieval is restricted to the Semantic Scholar channel with results_per_query= 2, so these parallel academic calls are not exercised; retrieval is then single rate-limited source, identical across backbones. 3.3 Model Serving and Decomposition Both models are run through Hugging Face runtimes. The same pipeline code drives all three configurations (diffusion full, diffusion fast, autoregressive), and only the backbone and the decompose mode change. The decompose call accepts mode of full or fast, and its output is accepted only when it parses as JSON with exactly the requested number of non-empty subqueries, which gives both modes the same correctness criterion. 3.4 Operating Modes Full mode. Full mode is ordinary diffusion generation. The decomposition prompt is built and the model is run to completion; the final text is parsed as JSON and accepted if it contains exactly the requested number of subqueries. This is the correctness-oriented configuration. Fast mode. Fast mode extracts the decomposition before final generation completes. The same prompt is issued, but custom streamer the inspects each intermediate denoising state: draft is decoded, stripped of thinking-channel artifacts, scanned for JSON object containing subqueries list, and accepted as soon as valid exact-count object appears. When early stopping is enabled, the streamer raises an exception that the decompose routine catches and returns the early subqueries instead of waiting for the final pass. This is not speculative decoding: the model is unchanged, and the only difference is that we read its own intermediate denoised states. The tradeoff is that an early draft may contain duplicated fragments or rough wording, but for retrieval, topical coverage matters more than exact phrasing.

sections.title: 4 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluate on Deep Research Bench (Du et al., 2026), benchmark of 100 PhD-level research tasks (50 Chinese, 50 English) spanning 22 fields, calibrated against statistical analysis of over 96,000 real-world user queries. We follow the benchmarks official RACE evaluation framework, which scores reports along comprehensiveness, insight, instruction-following, and readability, and reports an aggregate overall score; here RACE is run with cleaning, using Gemini 2.5 Pro as the evaluator. RACE scores in our controlled runs are reported on 01 scale. the For size backbones of same pipeline: controlled comparison we use comparable in two the diffusion model the google/diffusiongemma-26B-A4B-it (denoted dFull and dFast for its full and fast decomposition modes) and the autoregressive model google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it (AR). Both are run through Hugging Face runtimes on an H200 pod, with retrieval performed locally. All three configurations share the same agent code, retrieval (Semantic Scholar only, subquery_count= 4, results_per_query= 2, one request per second, per-request timeout), and RACE evaluation; only Mode mean p50 p90 vs AR AR dFull dFast 71.45 11.89 11.97 48.78 11.87 12.07 111.87 16.13 16.33 1.0 6.0 6.0 Table 1: End-to-end latency (seconds) over the 100 Deep Research Bench tasks. Both diffusion modes are about 6 faster than AR, while dFast provides no additional end-to-end reduction over dFull. the generator backbone and the decompose mode differ. AR uses standard left-to-right decoding with no draft-state stream. We additionally report separate isolated study of the decomposition stage on 100 synthetic-but-realistic research queries, instrumented directly through the diffusion streamer with model loading excluded from all timings. We additionally analyze the stored run artifacts without regenerating reports, repeating retrieval, or calling the evaluator. For every successful report we measure total non-whitespace characters, numeric inline citations, and Markdown content headings, and split these diagnostics and saved RACE scores by language. We also conduct configuration-blinded manual source-grounded audit of 10 reports from common-success tasks (5 English, 5 Chinese; dFull = 3, dFast = 3, AR = 4 after unblinding). Prompt requirements are fixed before reading reports; five material claims per report and all inline citation mentions are checked against the exact retrieved evidence available to the writer. This diagnostic is not expert human evaluation or an open-world factuality test.

sections.title: 5.3 Accelerating Decomposition
sections.content: Fast mode targets the decomposition stage specifically by reading intermediate denoising states. In the full pipeline this lowers mean decomposition latency from 0.62 (dFull) to 0.36 (dFast), about 1.7, and against ARs 3.69 it is roughly 10. To characterize the mechanism in isolation, we ran 100-query probe of the decomposition stage alone, with the model asked to return exactly six search subqueries as JSON, timing each query from the start of generation with model loading excluded. valid exact-count object appeared during denoising for all 100 queries, with mean of 8.99 draft steps (median 9, range 617). Table 3 reports the latency of three extraction points. Taking the first exact-count draft is 1.99 faster at the median than waiting for full generation (243.4 ms vs. 484.9 ms); requiring stable object (the same exact-count JSON observed for two consecutive states) is only 1.04 faster at the median but reproduces the final answer exactly in 91 of 100 cases, versus 1 of 100 for the first draft. In the current pipeline this is stage-level optimization, not an additional end-to-end speedup. 5.4 Report Quality faster pipeline is only useful if quality holds. Table 4 reports RACE scores under cleaning and the requested language-specific diagnostics. The diffusion fast mode obtains the best available-case overall score (0.3969), ahead of dFull (0.3895) by 0.0074 and ahead of AR (0.3904) by 0.0065. In the paired common-success analysis, every overallRACE mean-difference interval includes zero in both languages. Replacing autoregressive decoding with diffusion, and extracting decomposition from draft states, does not lower report quality, and it delivers the latency reductions reported above. 5 The descriptive length differences are much smaller than the latency gap: diffusion reports are about 1017% shorter than AR reports in the language-specific means, whereas the writer is about 1112 faster  (Table 2)  . Shorter outputs alone therefore cannot explain the writing-stage speedup. Manual source-grounded audit. Across the 10 blinded reports, 14 of 50 sampled material claims (28%) were fully supported by the retrieved evidence and 10 (20%) were partially supported; 26 (52%) were not established by the stored source packet. Of 76 inline citation mentions, 41 (53.9%) fully entailed the adjacent claim, 21 (27.6%) partially entailed it, and 14 (18.4%) did not establish it. Eleven of 22 cited sources were strong or adequate for the specific use. Prompt-facet coverage was high overall (87.4%; English 92.7%, Chinese 82.2%). The recurring failures were metadata-only or off-topic Semantic Scholar results, unsupported extrapolation, and missing quantitative evidence. These findings identify retrieval grounding as shared system bottleneck rather than decodingspecific effect; the per-mode audit samples are too small for comparative claims.

sections.title: 5.5 System-Level Leaderboard Snapshot
sections.content: The controlled study above uses two open models of comparable size to isolate the effect of the backbone. Separately, to assess end-to-end system competitiveness rather than isolate mechanism, we evaluated an instance of DiffResearch built on stronger diffusion model (Mercury (Inception Labs et al., 2025)) on the public Deep Research Bench leaderboard, where RACE is reported on 0100 scale. As Table 5 shows, this instance scores 48.03 overall, ranking above several publicly listed commercial systems at the time of evaluation, including OpenAI Deep Research (46.45), Dr. Tulu (45.49), and Claude Research (45.00). Its strongest results are on insight (48.20) and readability (47.40), the two dimensions most directly tied to long-form synthesis. Because leaderboard entries differ in retrieval infrastructure, model scale, and engineering investment, this time-specific snapshot supports system-level competitiveness claim only and does not attribute the ranking to diffusion decoding. 5.6 Discussion Our results support narrow but practical claim. Diffusion also exposes intermediate denoising states that can be read mid-generation. For structured intermediate output such as decomposition, these drafts are usable well before the final pass, which adds further 2 on that stage in isolation but no additional end-to-end reduction in the current pipeline. The source-grounded audit shows that this decoding gain does not solve retrieval relevance or evidence sufficiency, which remain shared bottlenecks. Separately, the public leaderboard snapshot shows that the complete Mercury-backed DiffResearch system is competitive with listed commercial systems, but it does not attribute that ranking to diffusion decoding. Thus, the controlled study supports the decodingparadigm latency claim, whereas the leaderboard supports end-to-end system competitiveness.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: The end-to-end speedups are measured with the model served on an H200 pod and retrieval kept local. On hardware or model configurations where local diffusion inference becomes the bottleneck, or where retrieval cost is small relative to generation, the absolute latency gap will differ; we have not benchmarked under tight consumer-grade latency budgets. Fast mode is deliberately scoped to decomposition and does not reduce observed endto-end latency relative to dFull in the current setup: the first exact-count draft rarely matches the final string exactly (1 of 100 in our probe), so it is appropriate only where downstream consumers tolerate 6 wording noise, as retrieval does, and not for the final answer. The controlled comparison uses two open models of comparable size; while it holds the scaffold, prompts, retrieval, and evaluation fixed, it is single backbone pair, and broader sweep across model families and sizes would strengthen the attribution. Finally, the leaderboard comparison is against full systems rather than writer-isolated variants and reflects snapshot in time; it should be read as system-level result, not causal attribution to diffusion decoding alone. Retrieval in these runs used Semantic Scholar only, which for some benchmark tasks did not return the sources the task needed; the academic channel can also use arXiv and the web channel, but both were disabled here. Parallel retrieval dispatch, which singlepass subquery generation enables in principle, is not evaluated here because retrieval is rate-limited to one request per second; quantifying it under higher-throughput retrieval backend is left to future work.
